sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Iterative sampling in diffusion models during inference can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real training images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. In this paper, we introduce correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base models own prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target as the base model. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoisers clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. We find that applying correction beyond the single step supervised during training is key to the significant quality gains. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We extensively evaluate our method across widely used architectures, including DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and unconditional generation. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion models generate images through sequence of denoising predictions (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020). At each sampling step, neural network estimates clean data from noisy input, and this estimate is used to update the sample. But one curious property of diffusion models is the Project page: https://sunovivid.github.io/correction-training/ 1 Figure 2: Denoising and prediction correction. During training, the denoiser and corrector predict the same clean target. Stop-gradient blocks the correction loss through the denoisers prediction. During sampling, each denoising prediction is refined times before the next sampling step. training-inference gap arising from what is known as exposure bias (Ning et al., 2023; 2024; Li et al., 2024a; Yu & Zhan, 2025). The denoiser is trained on real training images interpolated with noise. At inference time, however, it receives noisy inputs that depend on its own imperfect predictions from earlier steps. These inputs can differ from the noisy training inputs, creating mismatch between training and inference. As noise decreases along the denoising trajectory, prediction errors can accumulate, often producing visual artifacts and incoherent structures in the generated images. common way to improve sample quality is classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2022), which generates better quality samples, but at the cost of reduced diversity and oversaturation. In this paper, we take more direct approach: correcting the models own prediction. We introduce corrector that takes the base models prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target, as illustrated in Fig. 2. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we therefore iteratively correct the denoisers clean-sample prediction. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, we find that it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference time without additional training. This iterative correction further improves sample quality, producing sharper images with more coherent structures. We hypothesize that repeated correction helps compensate for errors accumulated over earlier denoising steps, reducing the denoisers traininginference gap and contributing to the observed improvement (see Sec. 4.2 for details). We evaluate our method across class-conditional, unconditional, and text-to-image generation, using established models including DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023), SiT (Ma et al., 2024), REPA (Yu et al., 2024), and JiT (Li & He, 2026). Correction improves unguided sample quality across these settings with relatively small amount of additional training. The gain remains at matched numbers of function evaluations (NFEs), suggesting that introducing correction steps can make more effective use of inference compute than denoising alone. In unconditional generation, correction also provides substantial improvements without any guidance signal. Comparisons with CFG on DiT and SiT show better quality at matched diversity, as measured by FID (Heusel et al., 2017) and recall (Kynkaanniemi et al., 2019). Qualitatively, correction shows less oversaturation and greater visual realism than CFG. Moreover, adding correction to CFG reduces the stereotypical AIgenerated look of its samples. We present conditional and unconditional samples using correction in Fig. 1. Finally, we show that the corrector can be made as efficient as standard diffusion models while retaining its quality advantage. We distill corrected predictions back into the base diffusion model. The student learns to match predictions obtained through repeated correction and requires only one forward pass per sampling step. The resulting model retains much of the quality improvement while preserving the base models architecture, parameter count, and inference cost. sections.title: 2.2 PREDICTION ERROR DURING SAMPLING
sections.content: Fig. 3 (a) illustrates how structural errors can persist along the sampling trajectory. Early predictions contain incoherent object structures. Later denoising steps add texture and facial details such as teeth, eyes, and tongue while largely preserving the incorrect object structure. The clean targets used for training, however, are real images with coherent object structures. The denoiser learns to recover these structures from noise, but is not explicitly trained to further refine its own predictions at the same noise level. One widely used way to obtain sharper, more coherent samples is classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2022). CFG strengthens conditioning by amplifying the difference between conditional and unconditional predictions. However, it can reduce sample diversity and produce oversaturated images. In this paper, we make prediction correction an explicit learning task: we train corrector Cϕ that takes the denoisers own prediction as input. During sampling, we apply this learned mapping repeatedly to improve sample quality. As we show in Sec. 4, repeated correction can improve generation even when it increases reconstruction error on training inputs. We investigate this behavior and its relationship to the traininginference gap. 3 Figure 3: Prediction correction improves structural coherence during sampling. We show clean-sample predictions ˆx along denoising trajectories without (a) and with (b) correction. In (a), early structural errors persist as later denoising steps add details. In (b), iterative correction revises the prediction at each t, producing more coherent object structures before the next denoising step. Each triplet shows this refinement within one denoising step. Additional visualizations are shown in Appendix D.2  (Fig. 34)  .

sections.title: 2.3 LEARNING TO CORRECT MODEL PREDICTIONS
sections.content: Standard denoising training learns the mapping zt by reconstructing images corrupted by prescribed noise process. Given noisy observation zt, the denoiser produces an initial prediction ˆx(0), which may still contain inaccuracies. We introduce prediction correction as reconstruction task that uses this prediction as its input. The corrector takes ˆx(0) and predicts the same clean target x, learning the mapping ˆx(0)  (Fig. 2)  . When ˆx(0) already captures much of the structure in x, the initial denoising pass has already performed much of the reconstruction. The corrector can then build on this estimate and focus on the remaining inaccuracies. We refine ˆx(0) by applying corrector Cϕ again at the original time t: ˆx(1) = Cϕ( ˆx(0), t). The corrected prediction directly estimates the clean sample x. We train it with Lcorr = Ex,ϵ,t (cid:104) Cϕ(sg( ˆx(0)), t) x2 2 (cid:105) , (4) where sg is the stop-gradient operation. Starting from pretrained denoiser, we jointly optimize Ltotal = Ldenoise + λcorrLcorr, where λcorr weights the correction task. The denoising term supervises the initial prediction, while the correction term supervises its refinement. sections.content: Training supervises only single correction step, from the initial denoising prediction ˆx(0) to the refined prediction ˆx(1). sections.title: 3 RESULTS
sections.content: We evaluate correction on class-conditional and unconditional generation (Sec. 3.1) and text-toimage generation (Sec. 3.2). We also demonstrate that the base and correction models can share most parameters and that additional correction passes can be eliminated with distillation (Sec. 3.3). We detail our experimental settings in Appendix B. 3.

sections.title: 3.3 MAKING CORRECTION EFFICIENT
sections.content: Parameter-efficient correction through weight sharing. The denoiser and corrector can share backbone while retaining separate lightweight input embedders, which contribute only small fraction of the total parameters. In the shared configuration, the backbone receives gradients from both the denoising and correction losses. We also compare against larger single denoiser with roughly matched parameter count, and find that iterative correction yields substantially larger gains than simply doubling the denoiser depth (Sec. 4.1, Tab. 7). sections.title: 4 DISCUSSION
sections.content: In this section, we investigate where the quality gains from correction might come from. We first compare denoisercorrector pair with single deeper denoiser containing the same total number of transformer layers (Sec. 4.1). We then empirically examine the behavior of iterative correction and its relationship to the traininginference gap (Sec. 4.2). Finally, we examine how the number of corrections seen during training and denoiser updates affect the quality gains from iterative correction (Sec. 4.3). 1https://www.rapidata.ai/

sections.title: 4.2 HOW ITERATIVE CORRECTION CHANGES PREDICTIONS AND SAMPLING
sections.content: Iterative correction sharpens the denoisers predictions. The corrector is trained to reconstruct the clean target from the denoisers prediction. Its output is another clean-image prediction, allowing the same mapping to be applied repeatedly at fixed noise level. We examine how this repetition changes the predictions. Fig. 13 shows this visually. We use noisy data zt = (1 t)x + tϵ as input to JiT-L/16 and show its predictions before and after correction. Repeated correction resolves ambiguous structures and makes faces, object contours, and other details more coherent. (b) In extreme cases, correction appears to push this coherence too far, turning ambiguous structures in the base prediction into overly regular geometric shapes. For example, in (a), the blurry, average-like predictions of dogs, pandas, and cars become distinct, well-formed objects. In (b), the corrector sometimes makes overly coherent structures, such as disk-like pizza toppings or strawberry seeds arranged in regular grid. In our from-scratch experiments, single correction yields similar FID to deeper, parametermatched denoiser (Sec. 4.1). However, repeated application of the same corrector substantially improves sample quality at matched inference budget. Our intuition is that splitting the computation into denoising and correction exposes refinement operation that can be reused. The denoiser first maps the noisy input into clean-image prediction, and the corrector learns to refine this prediction toward the original clean target. single correction may provide refinement similar to that achieved by additional denoiser layers. Repeated correction, however, reapplies this learned mapping to its own outputs, beyond the single iteration used during training. This may reinforce coherent structures, sometimes excessively, producing overly regular patterns such as the disks and grids. Does iterative correction reduce denoising error? Thus, even as predictions become sharper and more coherent, iterative correction can move them farther on average from the optimal denoising prediction. Iterative correction reduces the traininginference gap. How can iterative correction improve sample quality even when it increases denoising error? Denoising error is measured on noisy inputs drawn from the training distribution, whereas intermediate states encountered during sampling can follow different distribution (Song et al., 2025). Each corrected prediction is used to construct the next noisy state, which becomes the denoisers input. Thus, we hypothesize that correction may improve generation by bringing these states closer to the training distribution. We measure the traininginference gap using classifier two-sample test (Lopez-Paz & Oquab, 2016). We train classifiers to distinguish intermediate states zt from the training distribution, zt = (1 t)x + tϵ, from those along denoising trajectories at inference. Specifically, we experiment with SiT (Ma et al., 2024) on 100K intermediate states, and report binary cross-entropy (BCE) and AUROC on held-out datasets. smaller training-inference gap should make the two distributions harder to distinguish, bringing AUROC closer to 0.5 (random chance). Figure 15: Measuring the training inference gap with classifier twosample tests. We train classifier to distinguish samples from the training distribution and the inference distribution, and report AUROC and binary crossentropy (BCE). Overall, correction makes classification harder, indicating smaller gap between training and inference. As shown by the BCE in Fig. 15, the classifier can distinguish training and inference states, with classification becoming easier as the noise level decreases. This trend is consistent with errors accumulating during sampling due to exposure bias (Ning et al., 2024; 2023). Notably, single correction (gray lines) yields higher BCE and lower AUROC, suggesting that correction reduces the traininginference gap. Iterative correction generally reduces the gap further (blue lines), which may contribute to better sample quality even when reconstruction error on training inputs increases.

sections.title: 4.3 HOW TRAINING AFFECTS ITERATIVE CORRECTION
sections.content: Figure 16: Correction beyond the supervised training depth improves generation (lower FID). Supervising more correction steps shifts the best-performing tested inference correction count toward larger values, often approximately twice the maximum supervised depth. This suggests that extrapolating the learned correction beyond its training inputs may play an important role in the observed gains. Extrapolation is key to substantial quality gains. We denote the number of correction iterations applied during training by Ktrain. In our default setting (Ktrain = 1), the corrector sees only the denoisers initial prediction during training. We also train the corrector to predict the target after multiple correction iterations (Ktrain > 1). Increasing Ktrain shifts the best-performing inference correction count toward larger values, while the best achieved FID remains similar (Fig. 16, left). Notably, the best performance comes from applying correction more times than supervised during training. The right panel shows that increasing Ktrain lowers denoising error below the base denoisers only for correction iterations included in training. For > Ktrain, the error remains above this baseline, even at the correction count with the best FID. 12 Figure 17: frozen denoiser can support high quality refinement, but iterative correction can also oversaturate samples and produce abrupt changes in the sample prediction. Our intuition is that the corrector learns mapping toward the optimal denoising prediction. Supervising more correction iterations may simply spread this correction over more steps, so more inference iterations are needed to obtain similar gains from extrapolating the learned mapping beyond the iterations used during training. Denoiser updates affect iterative correction. To examine how denoiser updates affect iterative correction, we compare (a) jointly training the denoiser and corrector, our default setting in Algorithm 1, with (b) freezing the denoiser and training only the corrector under the same correction framework. Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 17, samples in (b) improve with correction but change more abruptly in structure and appearance, with slight oversaturation typical of CFG. Fig. 18 shows similar FID for both settings at = 5. With further correction, FID continues to decrease with joint training but increases again with frozen denoiser despite visually improved samples, similar to the trend at higher CFG scales. One possible interpretation is that, in (b), the corrector specializes in the errors of particular denoiser checkpoint, making it less robust to iterative application. In (a), the denoiser continues to evolve during training, exposing the corrector to broader range of errors. This may help the corrector generalize to its own outputs and remain effective across different correction counts K. sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Stacked generalization (Wolpert, 1992) trains higher-level predictor on held-out predictions of base models to improve generalization. In diffusion models, self-conditioning (Chen et al., 2022) uses previous clean-data predictions as additional denoiser inputs, and recent concurrent works extend this idea to iterative refinement in language modeling and structured reasoning (Yoo et al., 2026; Helbling et al., 2026). We train an explicit corrector on denoiser predictions and reuse it across correction iterations, without requiring the original noisy input. Idempotent Generative Networks (Shocher et al., 2024) also learn iterative mappings through an explicit idempotency objective. Our method retains the denoising objective and applies correction at each noise level to refine predictions before the sampling update. The most relevant work to ours is Schiff et al. (2026), which trains corrector on generated samples and applies it repeatedly during sampling in discrete diffusion for language modeling.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce correction training, which learns to correct diffusion models predictions using the original clean-data targets. Despite being trained for single correction, the corrector supports repeated refinement at inference. Experiments on class-conditional and unconditional ImageNet 13 generation and text-to-image generation demonstrate substantial improvements in sample quality. Correction can achieve competitive quality with guidance while better preserving diversity. Correction can also be distilled to remove inference overhead. Our analysis offers empirical insights into why correction works, but theoretical understanding of its effectiveness and iterative behavior remains an open question for future research.

sections.title: D DISCUSSION
sections.content: D.1 TRAINING AND CAPACITY CONTROLS Additional-training and capacity controls. We examine how quickly the corrector converges by comparing correction training with three baselines: continued training of the base denoiser and two deeper denoisers with different initialization schemes. We use the pretrained SiTREPA-XL/2 denoiser with 28 transformer layers from Tab. 1. For the deeper denoisers, we append 28 transformer layers before the final unembedding layer, matching the total number of transformer layers in the denoisercorrector pair. The added layers are either randomly initialized or copied from the pretrained denoiser, with the latter matching our corrector initialization. We train all configurations for 50K steps and report their progress in Fig. 30. We use single correction pass (K = 1) to isolate its benefit from the additional gains of iterative refinement. Figure 30: Correction improves generation quality beyond continued denoiser training or parameter-matched deeper denoisers. As can be seen in Fig. 30 (a) and (b), correction improves FID substantially faster over the 50Kupdate training window we used, whereas continued training and both deeper-denoiser controls improve much less. Importantly, this gain appears with only single correction pass: despite using the same total sequential transformer depth as the 56-layer denoisers, the D28 + C28 correction model achieves substantially better generation quality. These results suggest that additional training or model depth alone cannot explain the gains, pointing to an advantage of learning to refine an already structured prediction over learning directly from noisy observations. Figure 31: Matched effective depth. Correction outperforms deeper denoiser at matched effective depth per denoising step and inference budget, using fewer parameters. Iterative correction improves quality at matched effective depth. One might argue that the gain from repeating correction simply comes from increasing the effective depth within each denoising step. To test whether this is the case, we compare the 28-layer monolithic denoiser (D28) with 7-layer denoiser and 7-layer corrector (D7 + C7), using = 3 corrections to match the effective depth of the monolithic denoiser (7 + 3 7 = 28; Fig. 31). For this comparison, we train both configurations from scratch for 80K updates. Both use exactly 240 denoising steps and 6,720 transformer-layer evaluations per sample. Surprisingly, despite using roughly half as many parameters (346M versus 675M), the shallow denoisercorrector pair achieves lower FID@50K (4.21 versus 4.88; Tab. 7). This highlights that iterative correction does more than improve prediction accuracy through additional denoiser layers. 35 D.

To further characterize the changes induced by correction, we examine the frequency content of generated samples. Prior work (Yu & Zhan, 2025; Kobayashi et al., 2026) has reported lower subband energy in reverse-process samples than in forward-corrupted real data. This motivates examining whether correction recovers frequency components that are underrepresented in baseline samples. We compare the power spectra of samples generated with = 0, . . . , 10 correction iterations against those of real images. As shown in Fig. 36, the baseline samples exhibit spectral deficit, particularly at high frequencies. Increasing the number of correction iterations reduces this deficit, with = 6 yielding spectrum that approximately matches the real-image reference. Further iterations can raise both lowand high-frequency power above the reference, indicating that the effect depends on the correction count.
